# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's orbital period matches its rotational period, causing one hemisphere to permanently face its star. This phenomenon, common among exoplanets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme climate conditions in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is temperature contrast. The dayside, under perpetual stellar bombardment, can reach scorching temperatures of hundreds of degrees, while the nightside plummets toward extreme cold, potentially freezing out atmospheric gases entirely. In extreme cases, a planet's atmosphere may collapse as volatile compounds freeze on the dark side, stripping the world of its protective blanket.

However, atmospheric and oceanic circulation can moderate these extremes. Winds transport heat from dayside to nightside, while oceans—particularly deep ones—act as enormous thermal reservoirs. Climate models suggest that planets with dense atmospheres or substantial oceans may maintain habitable temperatures across much of their surface, with the terminator zone, the twilight band between day and night, offering potentially temperate conditions.

Tidal locking also influences atmospheric chemistry and cloud patterns. On some modeled worlds, permanent dayside cloud decks form at the substellar point, reflecting stellar radiation and cooling the surface. This feedback can actually help maintain habitability by preventing runaway greenhouse effects.
